Grok Bot and Claude Duet can both draft a deck, sort your mail, and wait for your ok. The useful difference is the shape of the product, not a brand preference.

Grok Bot is set up as a team of Bots. They share a cloud computer, can work in parallel, and you can turn a repeated job into a routine on a schedule you set. You can also talk to them in the Grok Bot apps, in X Chat, on X, or with a Team Bot in Slack.

Claude Duet is set up as one proactive agent in its own app. I checked Anthropic's Introducing Claude Duet page, and it says, "We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track." It comes to you with a morning brief from your Claude memory, skills, and connected apps, and it checks those apps through the day. It's a research preview on a waitlist for Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US.

I haven't run the same job in both, so I won't pick a winner on that overlap. Start with the job, then match it to the shape that fits.

The full comparison, with every source linked, is in the first reply.

note_tweet.text:
10 months ago I onboarded OpenClaw agents with 4 files.

Now I spin up a new Grok Bot in literally 4 seconds with a single click.

A deep dive into my bot onboarding process:

1. The profile (this replaced IDENTITY.md). I give it a name, a title, and a description. Each bot (profile) has 1 key job.

2. Shared memory (this replaced USER.md). My name, my time zone, all our different offers, our ICP, etc. Every bot sees it, so I never have to repeat myself.

3. A voice skill + behavior rules (this replaced SOUL.md). This gives Grok Bot my tone and boundaries. (Things like no em-dashes, draft only, no auto-sending, etc.)

4. Skills and routines (this replaced AGENTS.md). A skill is a playbook my bot follows to complete a task. A routine is the SCHEDULE on which that skill runs. For example my Sunday weekly plan skill runs every Sunday at 8am and plans my week in Todoist.

5. Teammates (no old file for this one, used to just be multiple OpenClaw agents). Each bot owns 1 job and can hand work off to the next. For example my Concept Bot pitches a YouTube idea, Craft Bot writes the script, then I can decide to post or not, then Analytics Bot pulls the numbers after. They share memory and the same skills (like my voice skill), so the drafts sound like me. When I edit a draft, Craft Bot writes the lesson down as a rule it follows next time.

It's way easier these days to not have to mess with a bunch of markdown files to update your agents.

But one thing from the OpenClaw era still rings true - having clearly defined processes/skills/routines up front means less micromanaging of your agents later.

note_tweet.text:
I built my outbound agency to $7M ARR with a full team of GTM engineers.

Harry Mason, one of our first employees (ex Head of RevOps at ColdIQ), is building his with 15 Grok Bots & 2 humans... on their own outbound so far: 25 campaigns in 60 days, 70,000 emails sent, 13 deals in the pipeline & 3 closed.

He was one of the best we had (top 2, depending on who's judging), so I had him walk me through the whole org chart:

1. Head of GTM

1 of the 2 lead bots. It looks at every channel, tracks which call to action works best and tells Harry every week what to scale.

→ It also trains the new bots.

2. Campaign Manager

Creates the campaign, adds the leads & runs it in Instantly (sequencing).

Some of their first campaigns went out with no first name... Harry had to shout at it in a voice note haha! It took ~3 weeks of corrections before it got good.

3. Ryan Replies

Every reply lands in one channel with who answered, which campaign it came from & a drafted response.

On their free list offer it autonomously builds the list with the ColdIQ MCP & sends it over. The prospect can have it in under 10 minutes.

(I ran this same play by hand when I started ColdIQ, and I couldn't build the lists fast enough)

4. Lenny List Validator

Compares every company with the clients they've already worked with. One of their most used bots.

5. Eddie Engagers

Pulls the people who engage with their LinkedIn posts via the ColdIQ MCP, then checks them for fit.

6. Content Cassandra

Scrapes 10 posts a day from people in their industry (400 so far) and checks each one again 24 hours later to see how it performed.

7. CRM Bot

The new one, bot #16. It catches the leads that never made it into the CRM.

→ Probably the biggest time saver bot Harry has ever built. And about as reliable as a sales guy updating the CRM, he says.

8. The rest of the team

- Email Reviewer (reviews the copy before it goes out)
- Newsletter Neil & an AEO & SEO bot
- Walter Website, Reporting Ronnie, VA Vincent, Frankie Follow Up and a client assistant
- An Operations Lead (the 2nd lead bot) runs that last group, plus Lenny, Eddie & the CRM Bot

For a new campaign, Harry picks the offer and the bots build the list (minus duplicates, competitors & existing clients). He checks the first 20 leads himself, presses approve & it loads into Instantly.

Then it runs on routines:
- Every day at 9:00 a.m. → new leads get added.
- Every Tuesday → 2 new campaigns launch.
- Every Friday → a report of what happened & what worked.

Writing the cold emails is the part Harry doesn't hand to the bots. His take is that AI ones say too much & run long, so the ideas stay with him.

I've been a heavy Claude Code user, and I believe Grok Bot will go completely mainstream because of how easy it is to use.

The full walkthrough is in the video below.
